analysis.one_liner: Phases out federal peanut quotas and caps government nutrition-program peanut purchases at world prices.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill with 49 cosponsors to phase out Depression-era peanut quotas never got a hearing or a vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1938, federal law has limited which farmers can sell peanuts for American food use, keeping domestic peanut prices well above world prices. This bill would have cut the government's price-support floor for quota peanuts, ended the quota system after the 2003 crop, and required the USDA to buy peanuts for school lunches and other food programs at no more than the world market price. It never received a hearing or a vote in the House.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, who pay above-world prices for peanut products under the quota system; taxpayers, who fund the price-support program; and the school lunch, food stamp, and food-bank programs that would have bought peanuts at world prices instead of inflated domestic ones. Non-quota farmers could also have sold peanuts for domestic use for the first time.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers, taxpayers, and school food programs

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the government's loan rate for quota peanuts from $610 per ton (2001) to $550 (2002) to $500 (2003), lowering the price floor the government sets under the program.

Repeals the peanut quota system entirely for the 2004 crop and after, which would end the licensing regime that restricts who may sell peanuts for domestic food use and keeps domestic prices above world prices.

Requires the Secretary of Agriculture to pay no more than the prevailing world market price when buying peanuts for the school lunch program, food stamps, food banks on Indian reservations, senior nutrition programs, and other federal food programs.

Replaces quota price supports with nonrecourse loans capped at $350 per ton, administered at no net cost to the Commodity Credit Corporation, so the successor program is far cheaper than the quota regime.

analysis.who_pays: Peanut quota holders — the farmers and quota owners whose government-created right to sell domestic-use peanuts carried real market value — would lose that asset outright, with no compensation in the bill. Growers in quota-heavy Southeastern districts would also face the loss of a protected, above-market market.

drawbacks.text: The bill eliminates quotas with no buyout or transition payments, even though quota rights were a valuable asset that holders had bought, inherited, or built farming operations around. An honest supporter would have to concede this was a hard, uncompensated hit on a specific group of farmers.

The bill does not end federal involvement: it replaces the quota program with a new nonrecourse loan program at 85% of recent market prices, which could still involve the Commodity Credit Corporation in holding and disposing of peanuts.

Requiring nutrition programs to buy only at world price could disrupt the processors and handlers who had supplied domestic peanuts to school lunches and food banks, since the entire domestic market had been built around quota prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers and taxpayers the gains are broad and ongoing — lower peanut prices across the whole food market and cheaper government food purchases — while the costs fall on a few thousand quota holders and quota-dependent growers. The design flaw is the absence of any buyout or transition aid for those holders, which is both a fairness problem and a political weakness; Congress ultimately addressed that flaw in the 2002 farm bill by paying quota holders to give up quotas rather than simply abolishing them.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Agriculture and Education and Workforce Committees, then to their subcommittees, and sat there until the two-year Congress ended without ever getting a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Representative Christopher Shays introduced the bill on June 13, 2001, with 41 original cosponsors from both parties.
The Speaker referred it to the Agriculture Committee and the Education and the Workforce Committee, splitting jurisdiction between them.
Within a week it was sent to the Specialty Crops and Foreign Agriculture Programs subcommittee, and that August to the Education Reform subcommittee; no further action of any kind is recorded.

By the time the bill was introduced, cosponsorship had grown to 49 members — 30 Republicans and 19 Democrats — but the bill never advanced past subcommittee referral for the rest of the 107th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Peanut quota holders and the quota-region peanut industry were better off because the bill died: the quota system that kept domestic peanut prices above world prices stayed in place through the 2002 crop, and Congress's eventual 2002 farm bill replaced it with a compensated buyout and a new federal support program rather than the uncompensated elimination this bill proposed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Peanut quota holders kept their federal rents

for.name: Christopher Shays
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to phase out peanut quotas and cap nutrition-program peanut purchases at world prices.

for.name: 30 of 223 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill to end the peanut quota program.

for.name: 19 of 208 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill to end the peanut quota program.

against.name: Larry Combest
against.what_they_did: The bill was referred to his committee and its specialty crops subcommittee and never received a markup or hearing; he instead advanced the 2002 farm bill, which replaced the quota program with a buyout and new federal supports rather than abolishing it outright.

against.name: Quota-state peanut interests
against.role: Southeastern peanut growers and quota holders
against.what_they_did: Defended the quota program, which they succeeded in preserving through the 2002 crop, when the next farm bill ended quotas only in exchange for roughly 11 cents per pound in buyout payments and a new federal price-support scheme.

sides.party_line_note: Support was genuinely bipartisan — 49 cosponsors split 30 Republicans and 19 Democrats — and the bill died in committee without any recorded vote, so there is no roll call to measure opposition.

industries.industry: Peanut quota holders and quota-region growers
industries.note: The bill would end the quota licenses that let a limited set of growers sell peanuts for domestic food use at above-world prices, wiping out the market value of those licenses. Their protected rents came directly out of higher prices paid by every American who buys peanut products.

Processors of peanut butter, candy, and other foods paid quota-inflated domestic prices for their main input; a free market in peanuts with world-price government purchases would lower their costs, savings that could pass to consumers.
